_note: Spot the Fallacy item bank. difficulty: 'easy' = everyday informal fallacies; 'hard' = formal, statistical and subtle ones. Each item's distractor_pool lists plausible confusions used to build the options.

items.text: You can't trust Dr. Lee's research on nutrition — she's overweight herself.
items.explanation: Her weight has no bearing on whether the research is correct — ad hominem.

items.text: Why listen to his budget plan? He failed maths in high school.
items.explanation: Old grades don't refute the plan itself — ad hominem.

items.text: My coworker says we should recycle more, but he drives a gas-guzzler, so his point is nonsense.
items.explanation: His hypocrisy doesn't make the recycling point wrong — ad hominem.

items.text: Don't take her film review seriously — she never even went to film school.
items.explanation: Lacking a degree doesn't invalidate the review's reasoning — ad hominem.

items.text: His argument about saving water is worthless — he's rich and has a huge pool.
items.explanation: His lifestyle doesn't disprove the argument — ad hominem.

items.text: Everyone at my school uses this app, so it must be the best one.
items.explanation: Popularity says nothing about quality — appeal to popularity.

items.text: Millions of people follow this diet, so it has to work.
items.explanation: Lots of believers doesn't make it effective — appeal to popularity.

items.text: This song is number one on the charts, so it's obviously the greatest song of the year.
items.explanation: Chart position reflects sales, not quality — appeal to popularity.

items.text: Most of my friends want to skip class, so it's clearly the right thing to do.
items.explanation: Friends agreeing doesn't make it right — appeal to popularity.

items.text: Everybody's putting money into this coin, so it can't be a bad investment.
items.explanation: Widespread hype isn't proof of a good investment — appeal to popularity.

items.text: Either we cancel the whole trip or we go completely bankrupt — there's no other choice.
items.explanation: There are options besides those two extremes — false dilemma.

items.text: You're either with us on this decision or you're against the whole team.
items.explanation: Disagreeing on one thing doesn't make you an enemy — false dilemma.

items.text: If we don't buy the newest phone, we'll be completely left behind in life.
items.explanation: Not upgrading isn't the same as being left behind — false dilemma.

items.text: We either ban screens for kids entirely or accept that they'll fail school.
items.explanation: There's plenty of middle ground between the two — false dilemma.

items.text: Either you finish the entire marathon today or you're not a real runner.
items.explanation: Runners exist between those two extremes — false dilemma.

items.text: The two Italian restaurants I tried were bad, so Italian food is just overrated.
items.explanation: Two meals can't judge a whole cuisine — hasty generalization.

items.text: My uncle smoked his whole life and lived to 90, so smoking clearly isn't harmful.
items.explanation: One case can't overturn the overall evidence — hasty generalization.

items.text: I met two rude tourists from that country, so people there must all be rude.
items.explanation: Two people don't represent a whole country — hasty generalization.

items.text: This brand's laptop broke on me once, so all their products are junk.
items.explanation: One failure isn't the whole product line — hasty generalization.

items.text: Both people I asked prefer tea, so basically everyone prefers tea over coffee.
items.explanation: Two people can't speak for everyone — hasty generalization.

items.text: A famous actor endorsed this supplement, so it must genuinely boost your memory.
items.explanation: An actor isn't a medical expert — appeal to authority.

items.text: My favorite streamer said this stock will moon, so it's a guaranteed win.
items.explanation: A streamer isn't a financial expert — appeal to authority.

items.text: A Nobel-winning physicist said this diet works, so it must be right.
items.explanation: Expertise in physics doesn't transfer to nutrition — appeal to authority.

items.text: The CEO said the product is perfectly safe, so there's no need to check any reviews.
items.explanation: The seller's own word isn't independent proof — appeal to authority.

items.text: A celebrity chef swears by this pan, so it has to be the best cookware for everyone.
items.explanation: One chef's endorsement isn't proof it's best for you — appeal to authority.

items.text: Every player on the team is over six feet tall. Sam is on the team. So Sam is over six feet tall.
items.explanation: The conclusion follows necessarily from the premises — it's valid.

items.text: If it rains, the match is cancelled. It's raining. So the match is cancelled.
items.explanation: A textbook valid step (modus ponens) — nothing is wrong.

items.text: Every book on this shelf is nonfiction. This book is on the shelf. Therefore this book is nonfiction.
items.explanation: The conclusion is guaranteed by the premises — valid.

items.text: The store is closed every Sunday. Today is Sunday. So the store is closed today.
items.explanation: The conclusion follows directly from the premises — valid.

items.text: She saves $200 every month. That's $2,400 over twelve months. So in a year she'll have saved $2,400.
items.explanation: The arithmetic follows from the premise — valid.

items.text: If a company is committing fraud, its auditor resigns abruptly. Kessler Ltd's auditor resigned abruptly last week. So Kessler is committing fraud.
items.explanation: Fraud would explain the resignation, but so would a fee dispute or a conflict of interest. Affirming the consequent.

items.text: Anyone who has genuinely understood the proof can reproduce it from memory. Priya reproduced it from memory. Therefore she genuinely understood it.
items.explanation: Memorisation also produces reproduction. The conditional never said understanding was the only route.

items.text: When a currency is about to be devalued, reserves fall sharply. Reserves have fallen sharply. A devaluation is therefore coming.
items.explanation: Reserves fall for many reasons — debt service, import shocks. The consequent doesn't establish the antecedent.

items.text: If the vaccine works, antibody counts rise. Antibody counts rose in the trial group. So the vaccine works.
items.explanation: Prior exposure raises antibodies too. Observing the consequent leaves the antecedent unproven.

items.text: If the bridge were over capacity it would show stress fractures. It isn't over capacity, so it won't show stress fractures.
items.explanation: Corrosion and fatigue crack bridges under capacity. Ruling out one cause doesn't rule out the effect.

items.text: If you train daily you'll improve. Marcus doesn't train daily. So Marcus won't improve.
items.explanation: Daily training is sufficient, not necessary. Three focused sessions a week could do it.

items.text: Firms that overstate revenue get delisted. This firm didn't overstate revenue, so it won't be delisted.
items.explanation: Delisting follows from many failures. Negating the antecedent says nothing about the consequent.

items.text: If it rained, the pitch would be unplayable. It didn't rain. So the pitch is playable.
items.explanation: Frost or a burst pipe would also make it unplayable. Rain was one sufficient cause among several.

items.text: The screening test is 99% accurate and Dan tested positive for a condition that affects 1 in 10,000. He almost certainly has it.
items.explanation: Among 10,000 people you'd expect ~100 false positives and 1 true one. A positive means roughly 1%, not 99%.

items.text: The facial recognition system is right 95% of the time and it flagged this traveller as a wanted suspect, so he's very likely wanted.
items.explanation: Wanted suspects are a vanishing fraction of travellers, so nearly every flag is a false positive.

items.text: She fits the profile of a professional violinist exactly, so she's more likely a violinist than a schoolteacher.
items.explanation: Schoolteachers vastly outnumber professional violinists. Representativeness is swamped by the prior.

items.text: Only 3% of applicants who interview badly are hired, so since Ana interviewed badly she's almost certainly not being hired.
items.explanation: That statistic runs the wrong way. You need the rate of bad interviews among those hired, against the overall hire rate.

items.text: Every founder profiled in this bestseller dropped out of university, so dropping out clearly improves your odds of building a company.
items.explanation: The book samples successes only. The dropouts whose companies failed were never eligible to be profiled.

items.text: These reinforced hulls always come back with damage along the flanks, so that's where the armour is doing its work.
items.explanation: You only inspect ships that returned. Hits elsewhere sank them, which is exactly where armour is needed.

items.text: Our alumni survey shows 92% satisfaction, so the programme clearly works.
items.explanation: The survey reaches those still on the mailing list. Anyone who dropped out or disengaged isn't answering.

items.text: Every long-lived building in the old quarter uses lime mortar, which proves lime mortar makes buildings last.
items.explanation: Buildings that used it and failed were demolished long ago, so they can't appear in your sample.

items.text: Players were sent to the sports psychologist after their worst game of the season, and nearly all improved next match. The sessions work.
items.explanation: Selecting on an extreme low guarantees improvement on average, with or without the intervention.

items.text: We audited the ten worst-performing branches, restructured them, and eight improved the following quarter. Restructuring is effective.
items.explanation: The worst quarter was partly bad luck, which doesn't repeat. You'd need a control group of untouched laggards.

items.text: Students scoring lowest on the mock were given the new tutoring and their real exam scores rose sharply, so the tutoring worked.
items.explanation: Picking the lowest scorers selects for people having a bad day, who drift upward regardless.

items.text: Shouting at the pilots after their worst landings clearly helps — they land better next time — whereas praising good landings makes them worse.
items.explanation: Exceptional performances in either direction are followed by more typical ones. The feedback is incidental.

items.text: Nothing is better than lifelong happiness. A cheese sandwich is better than nothing. So a cheese sandwich is better than lifelong happiness.
items.explanation: 'Nothing' means 'no thing is better' in the first premise and 'the absence of anything' in the second.

items.text: Evolution is only a theory, and theories are just educated guesses, so evolution is only an educated guess.
items.explanation: 'Theory' shifts from the scientific sense — a well-tested explanatory framework — to the colloquial one.

items.text: The law says everyone has a right to free speech, so the newspaper is legally required to print my letter for free.
items.explanation: 'Free' slides from 'without state restraint' to 'at no cost'. Two different senses.

items.text: Only man is rational. No woman is a man. Therefore no woman is rational.
items.explanation: 'Man' means humankind in the first premise and a male person in the second.

items.text: The document is authentic because it says so in its own preamble, and a document that declares itself authentic would hardly be a forgery.
items.explanation: The document's authority is what's in question, so its own testimony can't establish it.

items.text: Free markets produce the best outcomes, because outcomes produced by free exchange are by definition optimal.
items.explanation: The definition assumes the conclusion. Nothing is established that wasn't already granted.

items.text: He's trustworthy, because he told me he was, and he wouldn't lie about something like that.
items.explanation: His trustworthiness is the very thing his testimony is being used to prove.

items.text: This translation is the most faithful available, since the most faithful translation is the one our committee endorsed — and we endorsed this one.
items.explanation: Faithfulness is defined as 'what we endorsed', so the endorsement can't be evidence of it.

items.text: Every component in this aircraft is individually reliable, so the assembled aircraft is reliable.
items.explanation: Reliability doesn't compose — interactions and shared failure modes appear only in the whole.

items.text: Sodium is violently reactive and chlorine is toxic, so table salt must be dangerous to eat.
items.explanation: The compound's properties aren't the sum of its elements'. Division fails here.

items.text: The orchestra is the finest in Europe, so its second bassoonist must be the finest in Europe.
items.explanation: A property of the ensemble doesn't distribute to each member.

items.text: If every household saves more, the nation saves more.
items.explanation: Aggregate saving cuts spending, which cuts incomes — the paradox of thrift. What holds individually fails collectively.

items.text: No serious scientist doubts the hypothesis. — Professor Adeyemi doubts it. — Then she isn't a serious scientist.
items.explanation: The category is redefined to expel the counterexample, making the claim unfalsifiable.

items.text: Real fans never leave before full time. — Half the stand emptied at eighty minutes. — Those weren't real fans.
items.explanation: 'Real' is doing the work of excluding whoever disproves the claim.

items.text: A properly implemented version of the policy has never failed. Every failure you've cited was improperly implemented.
items.explanation: 'Properly implemented' is defined after the fact as 'didn't fail', so no evidence could count against it.

items.text: Nobody who truly understands the risks would take that bet. — Several risk analysts took it. — Then they didn't truly understand.
items.explanation: The counterexample is reclassified rather than answered.

items.text: Across forty measured outcomes the drug showed a significant benefit for left-handed men over sixty, so it works for that group.
items.explanation: Test forty outcomes and some cross significance by chance. The subgroup was chosen after seeing the data.

items.text: Three of the seven towns near the plant have elevated cancer rates, and drawing the boundary around those three shows a clear cluster.
items.explanation: The boundary was drawn around the hits. Clusters appear in random spatial data.

items.text: The strategy has beaten the index in eleven of the last fifteen years — we picked the fifteen-year window where it performs best.
items.explanation: Choosing the window after seeing returns guarantees a flattering record.

items.text: The prophecy mentions a great fire and a fallen tower, and looking back through the century I found a year matching both.
items.explanation: With enough years and loose criteria a match is certain. The target is painted afterwards.

items.text: Show me one peer-reviewed trial. — Here are three. — Well, none are longitudinal. — Here's a longitudinal one. — It isn't large enough.
items.explanation: Each standard is met and immediately replaced by a stricter one.

items.text: If he apologises publicly I'll accept it. — He apologised publicly. — He should have done it sooner, so it doesn't count.
items.explanation: The condition stated was met; a new one is introduced to avoid conceding.

items.text: No model predicted the crash. — This one did, in 2006. — But it didn't give the exact month.
items.explanation: The original bar was prediction, not month-level precision. It moved on being cleared.

items.text: Prove the software is secure. — It passed an independent audit. — Audits miss things; prove no vulnerability exists.
items.explanation: The demand escalates to an unmeetable standard once the stated one is satisfied.

items.text: Cities with more bookshops have higher literacy, so opening bookshops raises literacy.
items.explanation: Wealth and education levels drive both. The correlation has a common cause.

items.text: Employees who take the optional training get promoted more often, so the training causes promotion.
items.explanation: Ambition and manager support drive both taking the course and being promoted. Selection, not effect.

items.text: Neighbourhoods with more ice cream sales have more drownings, so ice cream is implicated in drowning.
items.explanation: Hot weather raises both. A third variable explains the association.

items.text: Patients who chose the private clinic recovered faster, so the private clinic gives better care.
items.explanation: Those who can choose it differ in income, baseline health and comorbidity. Not a like-for-like comparison.

items.text: The roulette wheel has come up black nine times running, so red is now overdue.
items.explanation: Spins are independent. The wheel carries no record of previous results.

items.text: We've had four failed launches in a row, so statistically the next one is far more likely to succeed.
items.explanation: Independent trials don't self-correct. If anything the failures are evidence of a systematic fault.

items.text: She's had three daughters, so the fourth is much more likely to be a son.
items.explanation: Each birth is close to independent. Prior outcomes don't shift the next probability.

items.text: This fund has underperformed for six straight years, so it's due for a strong run.
items.explanation: Being 'due' isn't a mechanism. Persistent underperformance may indicate a bad strategy.

items.text: One engineer says the dam will hold and another says it will fail catastrophically, so it will probably crack a little.
items.explanation: The truth isn't automatically the midpoint. One assessment may simply be correct.

items.text: The auditors say the books are fraudulent; the company says they're clean. The truth must be somewhere in between.
items.explanation: Splitting the difference isn't evidence. Either the fraud occurred or it didn't.

items.text: Some say the earth is 4.5 billion years old and others say 6,000, so a reasonable estimate is somewhere in the middle.
items.explanation: Averaging a well-evidenced figure with an unsupported one produces something worse than either.

items.text: Half the committee wants the bridge closed for repair and half wants it open, so we'll open it at half capacity.
items.explanation: If the structural case for closure holds, partial load doesn't address it. Compromise isn't a safety analysis.

items.text: If the alarm is armed the panel light is green. The panel light is not green. So the alarm is not armed.
items.explanation: Valid — modus tollens. Denying the consequent is legitimate, unlike denying the antecedent.

items.text: Every member of the committee voted against, and Reyes is a member of the committee, so Reyes voted against.
items.explanation: Valid — a universal claim applied to a member. This is instantiation, not the composition fallacy.

items.text: In the randomised trial, assignment was by lottery and the treated group recovered faster, so the treatment helped.
items.explanation: Valid — randomisation breaks the link with confounders, which is what makes causal inference legitimate here.

items.text: The specialist's claim is backed by three independent replications, so it's well supported — the replications, not her status, are the evidence.
items.explanation: Valid — citing an expert whose claim rests on replicated evidence isn't an appeal to authority.

items.text: The sample was drawn at random from the full register and is large enough for a 3% margin, so the estimate generalises.
items.explanation: Valid — random sampling with adequate size is exactly what licenses generalisation, unlike a hasty one.

items.text: Either the switch is open or it is closed; it is not open, so it is closed.
items.explanation: Valid — the two options really are exhaustive here, so this is disjunctive syllogism, not a false dilemma.
